learn.title: Wave Energy Converters
learn.intro: Harnessing the relentless motion of ocean waves offers a clean, abundant source of electricity that can complement solar and wind, helping nations meet net‑zero targets. Wave energy converters transform kinetic motion into power, reducing reliance on fossil fuels and enhancing grid resilience. By diversifying the renewable mix, wave technologies address intermittency, provide coastal communities with local generation, and support the broader energy transition toward sustainable, low‑carbon systems for future generations.
learn.c1_text: Wave energy converters come in several types: Oscillating Water Columns (OWC) use a vertical cylinder that rises and falls with waves, driving a turbine; Attenuators are long, floating structures that flex with wave motion; Point Absorbers are buoy-like devices that move up and down; Terminators are submerged structures that move with the wave surge. Each type captures wave energy differently, offering diverse pathways for renewable power generation.
learn.c2_text: The OWC is a simple yet effective design: a sealed chamber traps air as waves push water up and down, compressing and expanding the air to drive a turbine. This mechanical motion converts wave energy into electricity, with the turbine's rotation directly linked to the wave's vertical motion, making it a robust and scalable solution for coastal energy harvesting.
learn.c3_text: Point absorbers are buoy-like devices that move up and down with the wave, converting vertical motion into electricity through mechanical linkages. Terminators are submerged structures that move with the wave surge, using the horizontal motion to drive generators. Both designs harness different aspects of wave motion, expanding the toolkit for ocean energy conversion.

learn.title: Concentrated Solar Power (CSP)
learn.intro: Concentrated Solar Power (CSP) uses thousands of mirrors to focus sunlight onto a central receiver, converting heat into electricity. This thermal approach enables large‑scale, dispatchable power and integrates thermal storage, allowing electricity to be generated hours after sunset. CSP thus supports grid stability, reduces curtailment, and provides a reliable renewable source that can complement photovoltaic solar in the transition to clean energy for communities seeking resilient, low‑carbon power today now.
learn.c1_text: CSP uses thousands of mirrors to focus sunlight onto a central receiver, converting heat into electricity. This thermal approach enables large‑scale, dispatchable power and integrates thermal storage, allowing electricity to be generated hours after sunset. CSP thus supports grid stability, reduces curtailment, and provides a reliable renewable source that can complement photovoltaic solar in the transition to clean energy for communities seeking resilient, low‑carbon power today now.
learn.c2_text: CSP systems often include thermal storage, such as molten salt tanks, which retain heat for several hours. This allows electricity to be generated long after sunset, providing dispatchable power that smooths out solar intermittency and supports grid stability during peak demand periods.
learn.c3_text: India has 2.5 GW of CSP installed as of 2024, with the government targeting 30 GW of solar capacity by 2030 under the National Solar Mission. Major projects like the 500 MW Sakaleshwara CSP plant in Karnataka demonstrate CSP's role in India's renewable energy strategy, providing reliable power for industrial and residential use.

learn.title: Rooftop Solar and Net Metering in India
learn.intro: Rooftop solar empowers Indian households and businesses to generate clean electricity on-site, reducing dependence on imported fossil fuels and lowering electricity bills. By installing panels on rooftops, users can harness abundant sunlight while contributing to the nation’s renewable capacity targets. Net metering policies further enhance savings by allowing excess power to be fed back into the grid, making solar an economically attractive and environmentally responsible choice for India’s growing energy demand.

By installing panels on rooftops, users can harness abundant sunlight while contributing to the nation’s renewable capacity targets. Net metering policies further enhance savings by allowing excess power to be fed back into the grid, making solar an economically attractive and environmentally responsible choice for India’s growing energy demand.
learn.c2_text: Net metering allows solar system owners to receive credits for excess electricity fed back into the grid, offsetting their consumption. This mechanism makes solar installations financially viable by reducing net costs and encouraging wider adoption across residential and commercial sectors in India.
learn.c3_text: India installed 3.5 GW of rooftop solar by 2024, with net metering allowed in 12 states. The government promotes rooftop solar through subsidies and regulatory support, aiming to reach 40 GW of rooftop capacity by 2030 to meet rising energy demand sustainably.

learn.title: Solid-State Batteries
learn.intro: Solid‑state batteries replace liquid electrolytes with solid materials, dramatically improving safety by eliminating flammable leaks and reducing thermal runaway risk. Their higher energy density means more power can be stored in the same volume, extending device runtime and supporting longer‑range electric vehicles. This breakthrough promises faster charging, greater reliability, and a cleaner energy storage solution essential for the transition to sustainable transportation, enabling safer, greener mobility and clean future generations today.

learn.title: Duck Curve Problem
learn.intro: The "duck curve" describes how solar generation peaks midday and then falls sharply as evening demand rises, creating a steep ramp that challenges grid balancing. This pattern forces utilities to rely on costly peaker plants or energy storage to maintain stability during sunset hours. Understanding the duck curve is vital for integrating high solar penetration, ensuring reliable power supply, and designing markets that accommodate rapid fluctuations in renewable output for grid stability.

learn.c2_text: As the sun sets, solar output drops rapidly while electricity demand peaks, creating a steep ramp. Utilities must ramp up fossil‑fuel peaker plants or deploy battery storage to maintain grid stability, which increases costs and emissions during critical evening hours.
learn.c3_text: India's peak evening demand reaches 130 GW, while solar contribution drops from 30 GW at noon to under 5 GW at sunset, creating a steep ramp that requires rapid ramping of other generation sources or storage to maintain grid stability and avoid blackouts.
